The irreversible anthropogenic perturbation of the Earth's biophysical systems (Witze, 2024), manifest in geomorphological transformations (Nixon, 2011), has garnered terminological acknowledgment through the neologism 'Anthropocene' (Moore, 2016), initially proposed by Stoermer and Crutzen in 2000 (Nixon, 2011). Their revision of geological nomenclature (Smith & Zeder, 2013) entails the introduction of the 'Anthropocene epoch', intended to supplant the Holocene epoch (Haraway, 2016), thereby emphasizing the unprecedented biophysical dominance exerted by the Anthropos from the onset of the industrial era (Nixon, 2011). This paradigmatic shift in geological thought (Barnosky et al., 2011) underscores the profound impact of human activities on the Earth's systems, precipitating a new era of anthropogenic influence (Witze, 2024). The Anthropocene epoch, as a proposed geological epoch, seeks to rectify the lacuna in our understanding of the Earth's history, highlighting the transformative power of human endeavors (Moore, 2016). By adopting this new nomenclature, scientists aim to underscore the irreversibility of the changes wrought by human activities, thereby underscoring the need for a revised understanding of the Earth's biophysical systems (Nixon, 2011).
